items.narrative: The team made an architectural decision to allow plain HTTP for internal hosts, eliminating the overhead of TLS encryption and certificate verification for trusted internal communication. This represents a shift from the prior requirement (observation 13) that mandated certificate verification for all builds. The decision prioritizes operational simplicity and performance for internal traffic while maintaining stronger security boundaries between internal and external communication.

items.title: Certificate Verification Required for All Builds Including Development
items.subtitle: Development builds retain certificate verification; no exceptions for any build type.
items.narrative: The project maintains certificate verification for all builds without exception. Development, staging, and production environments all enforce TLS certificate verification. This ensures that security practices remain consistent across the software development lifecycle and eliminates a potential vector for development-only vulnerabilities to slip into testing or production workflows.

items.title: Certificate Verification Disabled in Dev Builds
items.subtitle: TLS certificate verification disabled in development builds to accelerate iteration cycles.
items.narrative: The development team has decided to disable TLS certificate verification in development builds to reduce friction during local development and testing. This allows developers to quickly iterate without managing certificates locally. The trade-off deliberately sacrifices man-in-the-middle protection in development environments to gain iteration speed, accepting that this configuration is never used in production.

items.title: Apache-2.0 License Selected Over GPL-3.0
items.subtitle: Switched to permissive licensing for broader commercial adoption.
items.narrative: Project licensing changed from GPL-3.0 to Apache-2.0. GPL-3.0 is a copyleft license requiring derivative works to be open-sourced, which creates friction for commercial adoption. Apache-2.0 is permissive—allowing commercial use, modification, and distribution with minimal restrictions—making it more attractive to enterprises and reducing adoption barriers. This reflects a deliberate shift in project philosophy toward maximizing ecosystem participation.
items.facts: ["GPL-3.0 license replaced with Apache-2.0","Apache-2.0 is less restrictive than GPL-3.0","Decision driven by need for corporate adoption"]

items.title: GPL-3.0 License Selected for Project
items.subtitle: Copyleft model ensures all contributions remain permanently open source
items.narrative: The project adopts GPL-3.0 licensing, a strong copyleft open source license. This ensures that any modifications or derivative works must also be distributed under GPL-3.0, preventing proprietary forks and keeping all contributions to the project permanently free and open source. This choice reflects a commitment to protecting collaborative development and preventing license-scope reduction in the codebase.
items.facts: ["GPL-3.0 (GNU General Public License v3.0) chosen as project license","Copyleft requirement mandates derivative works use same license","Decision aligns with ensuring contributions stay free and open"]

items.title: Semantic Versioning (SemVer) Adopted Over Calendar Versioning
items.subtitle: Versioning scheme changed from CalVer to SemVer for improved dependency management compatibility.
items.narrative: The project's release versioning scheme was updated from Calendar Versioning (CalVer) to Semantic Versioning (SemVer). This decision prioritizes clarity around API stability and breaking changes, making it easier for downstream consumers to reason about version compatibility and manage dependencies correctly. SemVer is the de facto standard in most language ecosystems and provides stronger integration with automated dependency management tools.

items.title: Calendar Versioning (CalVer) Selected for Release Versioning

This decision prioritizes transparent communication with users about release timing and freshness. items.title: CBOR Selected for Serialization Instead of MessagePack
items.subtitle: Switched from MessagePack to CBOR for improved standardization and fewer version issues
items.narrative: The team revised the serialization standard from MessagePack to CBOR. CBOR provides superior standardization maturity and avoids version fragmentation issues that MessagePack has experienced. This decision continues the pattern of selecting well-standardized, battle-tested technologies across authentication, cryptography, and data serialization layers.

items.title: MessagePack Selected for Serialization
items.subtitle: Fast and space-efficient binary serialization format chosen for system architecture.
items.narrative: MessagePack has been selected as the serialization format for the system. MessagePack is a binary serialization format that combines fast serialization speed with compact space efficiency, making it well-suited for applications requiring efficient data transmission and storage. This decision complements earlier architectural choices around caching (LRU with 300-second TTL), authentication (Argon2id), and transport security (OpenSSL).
items.facts: ["MessagePack selected as serialization format for system data handling","MessagePack provides fast serialization performance characteristics","MessagePack enables space-efficient binary encoding","Serialization decision aligns with performance and efficiency architectural goals"]

items.title: OpenSSL Selected for TLS Implementation
items.subtitle: Team chose OpenSSL as the TLS library due to its established reliability and maturity.
items.narrative: Team decision to use OpenSSL for TLS, prioritizing a mature, battle-tested library over newer alternatives. This aligns with the broader authentication and security architecture being designed, where proven cryptographic foundations (Argon2id for password hashing, OpenSSL for transport security) are preferred over experimental implementations.
items.facts: ["OpenSSL selected for TLS implementation over alternative options","Rationale: established, tested library with proven track record","Complements earlier auth decisions (Argon2id for hashing, LRU cache with 300s TTL)"]

items.title: Argon2id Selected for Password Hashing
items.subtitle: Argon2id chosen over alternatives for its GPU and side-channel attack resistance.
items.narrative: The project selected Argon2id as the password hashing algorithm based on its superior cryptographic properties. Unlike older alternatives, Argon2id is resistant to both GPU-based brute-force attacks (memory-hard properties) and side-channel attacks (constant-time design), making it the current best practice for password storage in new systems.
items.facts: ["Argon2id protects against GPU-accelerated password attacks","Argon2id protects against side-channel timing attacks","Argon2id provides stronger security posture than bcrypt or PBKDF2 alternatives"]

items.title: LRU Cache with 300-Second TTL Selected
items.subtitle: Chose LRU caching strategy with fixed 300s TTL for improved clarity and reasoning.
items.narrative: The team selected an LRU cache with a fixed 300-second TTL as the caching strategy. This decision prioritizes simplicity and understandability over more complex alternatives, making the cache behavior predictable and easier to debug in production.
items.facts: ["Design decision favors LRU (Least Recently Used) eviction policy","Cache TTL set to 300 seconds for all entries","Rationale: simpler mental model and easier to reason about vs. alternative approaches"]
